四.note: 四 first pictured breath leaving a nose; four was once just four lines, 亖.
四.history: The oldest way to write four was four strokes, 亖, like 一 二 三. In vertical writing those lines ran together with 二 and 三, so in the Spring and Autumn period scribes borrowed 四, a nose breathing out, for its sound. The breathing sense later moved to 呬, and 四 became the standard under the Qin.

八.note: 八 is two lines parting, "to divide", borrowed for "eight"; 分 and 別 took the old sense.
八.history: The two strokes of 八 bend away from each other: the first meaning was to divide. The word for eight sounded the same, so it took the character, and dividing moved to 分 and 別. The 八 at the bottom of 共 and 具 is something else, two hands holding an object, and under 真 and 典 it is the legs of a table.

乙.note: 乙's oldest gloss is fish guts, Heisig's keyword; as the second heavenly stem it means "second", B.

七.note: 七 is a cross of two cuts, first "to cut", a sense now written 切 with a knife beside it.

九.note: 九 first pictured an arm bent at the elbow, borrowed for its sound to mean nine.
九.history: 九 is a hand and forearm with the wrist bent, which is where the hook at the lower right comes from. The elbow sense moved to 肘, and 九 kept only the number. Once the arm was forgotten, an old explanation took over: a fist tightening as the count bumps up against ten.

月.note: 月 is a crescent moon, but in many kanji the same shape is meat or a boat.
月.history: 月 is a crescent, and 夕, evening, began as the same picture. Other kanji hold look-alikes: in 前 it was a boat, 舟; in 青 it was cinnabar, 丹; in 有, 然 and body words like 腕 and 腹 it is meat, 肉, which as a part is often written ⺼.

田.note: 田 is a field split into four plots; in 異 and 鬼 the same shape is a mask.

目.note: 目 is an eye turned on its side; in 買 the same shape is 罒, a net.
目.history: 目 is an eye stood upright, a quarter turn from the old picture, as also in 見 and 直. In 買 the top is 罒, a net gathering cowries, not an eye; and in 具 and 真 the 目 began as a cauldron, 鼎.

早.note: 早 first pictured an acorn, borrowed for its sound to mean "morning".
早.history: In the early bronzes 早 is an acorn. It was borrowed for "morning", and later forms rebuilt it as the sun, 日, over a sound part. The Shuowen read the 十 as 甲, "first": the sun's first appearance. That reading came long after the acorn, so it is the tradition rather than the history.

世.note: 世 is a sprig of leaves borrowed for "generation"; the old reading is three tens, thirty years.
世.history: 世 is 枼, the old form of 葉, leaf, without its tree: a sprig of leaves, borrowed for its sound to mean "generation". The Shuowen read it instead as three 十 joined together: thirty years, the span of one generation, and that is how it is often taught.

自.note: 自 pictured a nose, borrowed for "self"; the nose moved to 鼻, which still holds 自.
自.history: The oldest 自 is a nose, nostrils and all. It was borrowed for its sound to mean "oneself" and "from", and the nose was given a new character, 鼻, built on top of it. A folk story ties the two together: people point at their own nose to mean "me", as they still do in Japan.

中.note: 中 is a flagpole with a drum on it, set up in the middle of a field to gather people.
中.history: The oldest 中 is a pole with streamers and a box in the middle, read from finds as a drum. Set at the centre of a field or camp, it called people together and showed the wind. The Shuowen read it simply as a line through the middle of a box, and others see an arrow in a target.

朝.note: 朝 is the sun rising through the grass while the moon is still in the sky.

貝.note: 貝 pictures a cowrie shell, once used as money, so words about buying and wealth take it.
貝.history: 貝 is a cowrie, a small glossy sea shell that ancient China used as money. That is why money words carry it: 買 buy, 貸 lend, 財 wealth, 貿 trade, 贈 give. The 貝 in 則 and 員 was once something else that came to look the same: 鼎, a bronze cauldron.

員.note: 貝 is a round pot here, not money: 員 first meant round.

万.note: 万's old form 萬 pictured a scorpion, borrowed for its sound to mean ten thousand.
万.history: 萬 is a scorpion, borrowed for the number ten thousand; the scorpion later got its own character, 蠆, with 虫 added. Japan writes the short 万, a separate old character whose first meaning is unknown, already used for the number by the Spring and Autumn period.

具.note: 具 is two hands lifting a cauldron, 鼎: 目 is the pot and 八 the hands.
具.history: The oldest 具 shows two hands lifting a bronze cauldron, 鼎: preparing food, then any preparing, then tools. The cauldron shrank to 目 and the hands to the two strokes below. The Shuowen took the pot for 貝 and explained 具 as money.

右.note: 右 was a right hand alone; 口 was added later only to tell it apart.
右.history: In the oracle bones "right" was written 又, a right hand. Bronze scribes added 口 as a mark to keep it apart from the other words 又 wrote, and the hand narrowed into the shape on top. 左 is its mirror: 𠂇, a left hand, with 工 added.

有.note: 月 in 有 is meat, ⺼, not the moon; the hand above it narrowed as in 右.

則.note: 貝 in 則 was a cauldron, 鼎, perhaps for laws carved into bronze with a knife.

別.note: 口 and 勹 in 別 were once a bone, 冎: a knife cutting meat from the bone.

子.note: 子 is a baby: a big head, arms spread, and legs wrapped in a blanket.

女.note: 女 is a woman kneeling with folded arms; 母 is the same figure with two dots added.
女.history: In the oracle bones 女 kneels with folded arms, facing left. The modern shape faces right, and its loop is what is left of one arm; the other arm has gone. In the earliest texts 女 also wrote "mother", until two dots were added to make 母.

兄.note: 兄 is a mouth over a person: the elder brother is the one who gives the orders.

多.note: 多 is two pieces of meat, not two evenings: 夕 is a later look-alike.
多.history: In the oldest forms 多 is two pieces of meat, 肉. In the bronzes the meat was drawn like 夕, evening, and that look stuck. One reading is that meat was scarce, so two pieces was plenty; another is that a doubled sign means "many", as 木 doubled makes 林.

名.note: 名 is traditionally a mouth in the moonlight: saying your name to be known in the dark.

石.note: 石 first pictured a stone chime; the 口 under it was added as decoration.

光.note: 光 is fire over a kneeling person: ⺌ was the fire and 兀 the person.

原.note: 原 is a spring bursting from a cliff, so "source"; 源 took that sense with water added.

活.note: 氵 because 活 first meant the sound of flowing water.

泊.note: 氵 because 泊 first meant a boat at anchor; staying the night came later.

寺.note: 寺 first meant "to hold", now 持: 寸 is a hand and 土 was once 之, a foot.

点.note: 灬 is the bottom of 黑, black, in the old form 點: a black dot.

魚.note: 灬 is the fish's tail, not fire.

黒.note: In the bronzes 黒's old form 黑 is a figure with dots on its head, usually read as a tattooed face.
黒.history: In the bronzes 黑 is a figure with a large head marked with dots, usually read as the tattoos branded on a criminal's face, a punishment later called 墨刑 after 墨, ink, which holds 黒 itself. The oracle-bone form is uncertain. Japan's 黒 joins the old form's two dots in the middle into one stroke.

同.note: 同 first pictured a pipe, the sense now written 筒 with bamboo on top.

向.note: 向 is a mouth in a house, an echo, the sense now written 響; "facing" was borrowed.

若.note: 若 first pictured a person combing their hair; the 艹 on top is not grass.

暮.note: 莫 alone was the sun setting in the grass; when 莫 was taken for "not", 暮 added a 日.

兆.note: 兆 is traditionally the cracks in a heated shell read as an omen.
兆.history: Diviners heated a turtle shell or ox bone and read the cracks, and the Shuowen took 兆 for a drawing of those cracks: an omen. The oracle bones themselves show something else, two people turning their backs on a flood. Both readings fit the sense of a sign of things coming.

然.note: 灬 because 然 first meant to burn; "so" was borrowed, and 燃 took burning back.
然.history: 然 is 肰, dog meat, over 火, fire: to burn, as when meat is roasted. It was borrowed for "so, like that", and burning moved to 燃, which adds another fire beside it. The 月 at the top left is the meat, turned on its side.

茶.note: 茶 is 荼, a bitter herb, with one stroke dropped to make a character for tea.

王.note: 王 pictured a ceremonial axe, the king's symbol; heaven, man and earth joined is folklore.
王.history: The oldest 王 is the blade of a ritual axe, perhaps of jade, kept by the throne as a sign of the king's power. The old explanation reads three lines for heaven, people and earth, with the king as the stroke joining them, but the early forms are an axe. 士, a war axe, is its relative.

玉.note: 玉 was drawn almost like 王, so a dot was added to tell jade from king.

理.note: 理 first meant to polish jade, 玉, which is the 王 on its left.

主.note: 主 merges three old pictures: a lamp's flame, now 炷, burning wood, and a spirit tablet.

注.note: 氵 because 注 first meant to pour; attention is pouring your mind into it.

金.note: 金's two dots are lumps of metal; it meant copper first, then any metal, then gold.
金.history: 金 is a sound part, 今, on top of an axe-like sign, with two lumps of metal beside it, later the two dots. It first meant copper, the metal used before bronze, then metal in general, and only then gold. The Shuowen read it as metal buried in the earth, but the oldest forms have no earth in them.

前.note: 前 was a foot on a boat moving forward: 䒑 is the foot, 月 the boat.
前.history: The old form 歬 is a foot, 止, on a boat, 舟: moving forward. In the modern shape the foot has become 䒑 and the boat 月. The knife, 刂, came from a variant that first meant "to cut", now written 剪, and the two merged.

各.note: 各 is a foot, 夂, coming to an entrance, 口: arriving; "each" came later.

夢.note: 夢's 艹 is eyebrows, 罒 the eyes and 冖 the body of a sleeper, with 夕, night, below.
夢.history: In the oracle bones 夢 is a person lying on a bed, the eye sometimes drawn large and the hands restless. The bronzes dropped the bed, gave the eye its eyebrows and added 夕, night. Today the eyebrows are the 艹 on top, the eye 罒, and the body 冖.

士.note: 士 pictured a war axe; it came to mean the soldier, then the scholar-official.

周.note: 周 pictured carved jade, first "to carve", now 彫; it became a country's name.

売.note: 売's 士 was once 出, out: 出 over 買, buying turned outward, is selling.
売.history: The old form of "sell" was 出 over 買: buy, with "out" on top, so the same deal seen from the other side. 出 slowly wore down into 士, which has nothing to do with it, giving 賣, and Japan cut that down to 売. 読 has a right side that looks the same but began as a different sound part.

学.note: 学's ⺍ is what's left of two hands around crossed sticks, from the old form 學.
学.history: The old form 學 is built from 爻, crossed sticks, and 六, both thought to give the sound. Two hands, 𦥑, were later added around the sticks and a child, 子, below. In the modern form 六 wore down into 冖, and Japan's 学 shrank the hands and sticks to ⺍.

書.note: 書 is a brush, 聿, over 者 for the sound; the 日 is what's left of 者.

話.note: 舌 in 話 is not a tongue: it was 𠯑, a sound part that came to look like 舌.

読.note: 読's right side looks like 売, sell, but began as a different sound part that merged with it.

成.note: 成 is an axe, 戊, with 丁 for the sound, read as city walls, a sense now in 城.

止.note: 止 is a footprint, first "foot"; stopping came later, and 趾 kept the foot.

歩.note: 歩 is two footprints, one in front of the other; the bottom is a foot, not 少.

正.note: 正 is a foot, 止, under 丁 for the sound: first "to march on", now written 征.

走.note: 走 is a running figure over a foot; its 土 was the runner, 夭, not soil.

建.note: 建 is a hand setting a pole into a base; the right side looks like a brush, 聿, but isn't.

衣.note: 衣 is the collar and front of a robe, and it opens up to hold another part, as in 裏.

初.note: 初 is a knife and cloth: the first step in making clothes is the cut.

制.note: 刂 because 制 first meant cutting wood to shape, then to control.
制.history: 制 is 朱, a tree, beside a knife: cutting wood to shape. The tree is what became the 牛 and 巾-like strokes on the left. Shaping by cutting became setting rules and controlling, and 製 adds 衣, clothes, for making things.

雲.note: 雲 was first just 云; when 云 was borrowed for "to say", 雨 was added on top.

音.note: 音 is 言, speech, with a stroke inside the mouth, read as a muffled sound.

章.note: 章 is a chisel, 辛, through a piece of jade, now 日: first "to work jade".

帝.note: 帝 first pictured the base of a flower, now 蒂, and wrote the name of the highest god.
帝.history: The earliest 帝 is a whole flower: the head, its stamens, a stalk, and a mark where they join; the plant sense lives on in 蒂. On the oracle bones it already wrote the supreme god, who sent rain, thunder, harvests and illness. It also wrote a sacrifice offered to the four quarters, rivers and mountains. From there it became a title for kings, and later for emperors.

北.note: 北 is two people back to back, first "back", a sense 背 now holds with ⺼ added.

腹.note: 月 is the radical form of 肉, meat, not the moon: body parts take it.

欠.note: 欠 is a kneeling person with mouth open, which is why 歌 sing and 吹 blow hold it.

次.note: 次's 冫 is breath or spit leaving a person's mouth, not ice.

曽.note: 曽 pictured a steamer for cooking, borrowed for "once, ever"; 甑 kept the pot.

東.note: 東 looks like the sun behind a tree, but its oldest form is a sack tied at both ends.
東.history: The oldest 東 is a full sack tied at both ends. With a person carrying it, the same picture became 重, heavy; without one, it was borrowed for "east". The well-known reading, the sun (日) rising behind a tree (木), comes from the Shuowen, a dictionary of about 100 AD written long after the sack was forgotten. Scholars now call the tree a folk etymology, but it still works for remembering the shape.

虫.note: 虫 first pictured a snake; insects were 蟲, three of them, until 虫 stood in.

風.note: 風's 虫 is not an insect but a phoenix feather: wind was first written 鳳, the phoenix.
風.history: The oracle bones wrote wind with 鳳, the phoenix, borrowed for its sound, sometimes with 凡 added to give it. Later scripts kept 凡 and only a feather of the bird, and in the Qin script the feather was miscopied as 虫. The Shuowen, seeing 虫, tied wind to insects.

己.note: 己 pictured a cord for tying things, borrowed for "self"; 紀 kept the cord.

包.note: 包's inner part is an unborn child, 巳, wrapped in 勹, the womb.

電.note: 電 is rain over 申, a bolt of lightning: first lightning, now electricity.

家.note: 家 is a roof over a pig, but the pig, a boar in the oldest form, was there for its sound.
家.history: In the oracle bones 家 is a roof over 𢑓, a boar, which gave the word its sound. The boar was later drawn as 豕, an ordinary pig, and the story of pigs kept in the house grew from that. The Shuowen also read the pig as a sound part.

美.note: 美 is a person, 大, wearing a tall headdress of feathers or horns, now written 羊.

洋.note: 氵 because 洋 is the ocean; 洋服 are clothes from across the sea.

着.note: 着 is a miswritten 著: its 䒑 was 艹 and its 目 was 日.

進.note: 進 is a bird walking, traditionally because a bird can't step backwards.

雑.note: 雑's 九 is a shortcut for 衣, clothes, over 集: cloth of many colours put together.

準.note: 氵 because 準 first meant a water level; standard came later.

干.note: 干 pictured a shield; "dry" came from standing in for 乾.

午.note: 午 pictured a pestle, now written 杵; noon came through the old count of hours.

習.note: 習 is wings over the sun, 日, later 白: a young bird practising its flight.

国.note: 国 holds 玉, jade, only in the new form; the old 國 had 或 inside its border.

志.note: 志's 士 was once 之, there for the sound; it has nothing to do with the warrior 士.

思.note: 思's 田 was 囟, the soft spot on a baby's head: perhaps head and heart together.

意.note: 意's top only looks like 音, sound; one old form is 言 with 中 inside.

必.note: 必 is not 心: it likely pictured a weapon's handle, borrowed for "must".
必.history: Bronze forms likely show 必 as the shaft that holds a blade, the handle seen in 戈 and 戉, standing alone with two strokes added beside it. It was borrowed for "must, certainly", and over time it came to look almost exactly like 心, the heart, which it has nothing to do with. The stroke order still gives it away: 必 is not written like 心.

我.note: 我 first pictured a weapon with three blades, borrowed for its sound to mean "I".
我.history: The oldest 我 is a polearm with a three-pronged blade, a cousin of 戈, the one-bladed halberd it still holds. It was borrowed for the word "I" as early as the oracle bones, and the weapon was forgotten. The popular reading, a hand holding a weapon to defend oneself, is a later folk explanation.

義.note: 羊 in 義 stands for good and fitting, not for a sheep; 我 gives the sound.

才.note: 扌 is not a hand here: 才 pictured a sharp peg, borrowed for "talent".

存.note: 亻 is not a person here: it is part of 才, which gives 存 its sound.

又.note: 又 is a right hand, first "right"; borrowed for "again", it left "right" to 右.

友.note: 友 is two right hands, 𠂇 and 又: by the old reading, friends lending a hand.

支.note: 支 is a hand, 又, holding a bamboo branch; its 十 is half of 竹.

叔.note: 叔 is a hand with a digging stake, borrowed for its sound to mean "uncle".

爪.note: 爪 is a hand reaching down from above, more a human hand than a claw; ⺤ is the same.

将.note: ⺤ is not a claw here: the old form 將 has meat, 月, in that place.

受.note: 受 is two hands, ⺤ and 又, passing something across; 冖 was perhaps a boat, 舟.

愛.note: ⺤ is not a claw here: it is what is left of 旡, which gives 愛 its sound.
愛.history: 愛 was first 㤅: 旡 for the sound over 心, the heart. By the Qin a foot, 夊, had been added under it, as in 憂, and the 旡 later wore down into ⺤ and 冖. So in 愛 only the heart in the middle means anything, and neither the claw nor the cover is one.

広.note: 広's 厶 replaced 黄 in the old form 廣, a Japanese shortcut first seen in 1891.

弁.note: 弁 is two hands, 廾, putting on a cap, 厶; Japan also uses it for 辨, 辯 and 瓣.

台.note: 台 stands in for 臺, a tall lookout tower; 台 itself was once a separate word.

治.note: 氵 because 治 was first the name of a river; governing came later.

去.note: 去's 土 was a person, 大, and 厶 an opening: one reading is someone leaving a cave.

法.note: 氵 is traditionally explained as law keeping things level, like water.
法.history: The old form 灋 had three parts: water, 廌, a horned animal, and a sound part that wore down into 去, so the 去 in 法 does not mean "go". The animal was dropped later. In the earliest bronzes the character mostly wrote a word for "waste". The traditional story says law is level like water, and that the horned beast butted the guilty party at a trial.

会.note: 会 is 會 written in cursive, so its 云 has nothing to do with clouds.

至.note: 至 is an arrow landing point-down in the ground: to arrive.

出.note: 出 is a foot, 止, stepping out of a pit, 凵, not two mountains.

込.note: 込 was made in Japan: 入, going in, on ⻌, movement.

公.note: 公 is traditionally 八, turning away, over 厶, private: the opposite of private.

常.note: 常 was first a skirt, 巾 being the cloth; "always" was borrowed, and 裳 kept the skirt.

取.note: 取 is a hand, 又, holding an ear, 耳: hunters took the left ear of their kill.
取.history: An old ritual book, the Rites of Zhou, says that hunters took the left ear of the game they caught, to count it. 取, a hand holding an ear, is that taking. The Shuowen said the ears were cut from enemies in war, but there is no sign this was done.

最.note: 最's 日 was once a roof, 宀, over 取: first "to gather".

漫.note: 氵 because 漫 first meant water spreading without end.

買.note: 買 is a net, 罒, over a cowrie, 貝: gathering shell money in.

夫.note: 夫 is 大, a grown man, with a stroke added, traditionally the hairpin worn from age 20.

替.note: 替's two 夫 were two 立, standing figures, trading places.

臣.note: 臣 is an eye stood upright, looking down; it came to mean a servant, then a minister.

行.note: 行 is a crossroads seen from above; 彳 is its left half.

秋.note: 秋 first pictured a cricket or locust, sometimes over fire; 禾 and 火 came later.
秋.history: On the oracle bones 秋 is an insect, a cricket or a locust, sometimes with 火 underneath. Later it was rebuilt as 禾, grain, beside a sound part shortened to 火. The common explanation, burning the fields after the harvest to kill locusts and their eggs, joins the two.

利.note: 刂 because 利 first meant a blade cutting grain: sharp, then profit.

笑.note: 笑 was once 艹 over 犬, grass and a dog; 竹 and 夭 came later.

答.note: 答 was first 荅, with 艹 on top; 竹 replaced it by mistake.

体.note: 体 is 亻 and 本, root; the old form 體 had 骨, bone.

伝.note: 伝's 云 replaced 專 in the old form 傳, a Japanese shortcut, as in 転.

宿.note: 宿's 百 was a bamboo mat: a person, 亻, lying on it under a roof.

保.note: 保 is a person carrying a child on their back: 呆 is the child, its last two strokes the hand.

化.note: 化 is a person standing beside a person upside down: a turn, a change.

何.note: 亻 because 何 first pictured a person carrying a load; "what" borrowed it.

荷.note: 艹 because 荷 was the lotus; load was borrowed.

丙.note: 丙's first meaning is lost; as the third heavenly stem it means "third", the C after 甲 and 乙.

肉.note: 肉 is a slab of meat with its ribs; beside other parts it shrinks to 月.

傘.note: 傘 is a picture of an open umbrella, not people sheltering under one.

年.note: 年 is a person carrying grain, 禾: first the harvest, then the year.

夜.note: 夜's 亠 and 亻 are the remains of 亦, there for the sound, beside 夕, night.

易.note: 易 is not a lizard, as folklore says, but a full vessel: to give, a sense now in 賜.

戻.note: 戻's 大 was 犬, a dog, bending to slip under a door, 戸.

示.note: 示 is an altar; as a part it shrinks to 礻, in kanji about gods and rites.

社.note: 礻 because 社 was a shrine to the god of the land; companies came later.

祭.note: 祭 is a hand, 又, laying meat, ⺼, on an altar, 示.

甲.note: 甲 pictured a shell or plate armour; as the first heavenly stem it also means "first", A.

申.note: 申 is a bolt of lightning, the first form of both 電, lightning, and 神, god.

果.note: 果 is fruit on a tree, 木; the 田 is the fruit, not a field.

折.note: 折's 扌 is not a hand: it was a tree split in two, beside an axe, 斤.

雪.note: 雪's ⺕ is what's left of 彗, a broom, there for the sound under 雨, rain.

事.note: 事 is a hand, ⺕, holding a flagpole like the one in 中: doing one's job.

半.note: 半 is 八, to divide, over 牛, a cow: an ox cut in two.

不.note: 不 pictured the base of a flower, borrowed for "not".
不.history: The oldest 不 is a flower's calyx, the green cup under the petals. Adding 口 made 否, "no", and the negative sense flowed back into 不, until the calyx needed a new character, 柎. The Shuowen read it as a bird flying up toward the sky, 一, that it can never reach.

知.note: 知's 矢 was once 大, an adult, talking, 口, to a child: passing on knowledge.
知.history: On the oracle bones 知 and 智 were one character: 大, a grown person, 口, a mouth, and 子, a child, read as knowledge handed down. In the Warring States period 大 was miscopied as 矢, an arrow, which then gave the sound, and Western Han scribes dropped the child, leaving 矢 and 口.

予.note: 予 is a worn-down 呂 borrowed for "I"; Japan also uses it for 豫, "in advance".

柔.note: 柔 is a tree with soft, bending branches; the top only came to look like 矛, a spear.

帰.note: 刂 is not a knife here: it is what 帰 kept of the left side of its old form 歸.
帰.history: The old form 歸 has 𠂤, an early form of 師, troops, and 帚, a broom: sweeping away the enemy and coming home. A foot, 止, was added in the bronzes. 帰 squeezes the whole left side into two strokes, a shortcut first seen in a Yuan-dynasty dictionary, which is why it looks like 刂.

弟.note: 弟 is a strap wound turn after turn around a spear shaft: order, then the younger.

身.note: 身 pictured a pregnant woman, the body shown full.

射.note: 射's 身 is not a body: it was a bow with its arrow, and 寸 the hand drawing it.

教.note: 教's left side is not 孝: it is 爻, the sound, over 子, a child, beside a hand with a cane.

者.note: 者's 耂 has nothing to do with 老: 者 pictured sugarcane, or something boiling, borrowed.

阜.note: 阜 is a row of steps cut into a hill; on the left of a kanji it shrinks to ⻖.

交.note: 交 is a person standing with legs crossed, so "cross" and "mix"; its 父 is a look-alike.

練.note: 糸 because 練 first meant boiling silk soft; practice came later.

絵.note: 糸 because 絵 first meant embroidery.

終.note: 糸 for the end of a thread.

経.note: 糸 for the warp threads of a loom; passing through came later.

約.note: 糸 because 約 first meant tying with cord; a promise binds.

細.note: 細's 田 was 囟, a sound part, not a field.

後.note: 後 is a foot, 夂, held back by a cord, 幺: lagging behind.

服.note: 月 is not the moon here: it began as 凡, a tray, miscopied as 舟, a boat.

腕.note: 月 is the radical form of 肉, meat, not the moon: body parts take it.

興.note: 興 is four hands lifting something together, now 同 in the middle.

豆.note: 豆 pictured a tall bowl on a stand, borrowed for the word "bean".

盗.note: 盗 is 次, once drool, over a bowl, 皿: coveting what's in someone else's dish.

温.note: 温's right side is a person in a tub of warm water; 氵 was added later.

塩.note: 塩 is Japan's short form of 鹽: 土 replaced 臣, and 口 replaced 鹵, salt.

即.note: 即 is a person kneeling, 卩, at a bowl of food: coming up to eat, so near, so at once.

退.note: 退's 艮 was a food bowl: a foot walking away from the meal.

飲.note: 飲 was a person bent over a jar of wine, tongue out; 欠 is what's left of the drinker.
飲.history: On the oracle bones 飲 is a person bending over a wine jar, 酉, mouth open and sometimes tongue out, with drops falling. In the bronzes the mouth came loose and turned into 今 while the body became 欠, both now giving the sound. Clerical script swapped the jar for 食, food, which is the 飠 on the left today.

辛.note: 辛 is traditionally a chisel for marking criminals; the oldest forms may be young shoots.

新.note: 新 is an axe, 斤, chopping wood: first "firewood", now 薪; "new" was borrowed.
新.history: The left side of 新 is young tree shoots, 辛, with 木, wood, added below in the bronzes, and the axe beside them cuts them for fuel. The word for "new" sounded the same and took the character, and firewood moved to 薪, which adds 艹 on top.

報.note: 報's 幸 was 㚔, handcuffs, beside a hand forcing someone down: a sentence, then repay, then report.

寒.note: 寒 is a person in a house, bedded down in straw against the cold; 冫 is ice.

青.note: 青's 月 is not the moon: the old reading has 丹, red cinnabar, used for dye.

表.note: 表 is 衣, a garment, with 毛, fur, on the outside: the surface.

星.note: 星's 日 was 晶, three twinkling stars; 生 was added for the sound.

漢.note: 氵 because 漢 was the Han river, which named a dynasty and then China.
漢.history: 漢 is water plus a sound part, and its oldest use, on a bronze vessel from about 1000 BC, is the name of the Han, a river that runs into the Yangtze. The Han dynasty took its name from the land along that river, and centuries later 漢 became a name for the Chinese people themselves. Japan took it in that sense: 漢字 are "Han characters", Chinese writing.

難.note: 難 first named a kind of bird, 隹; "difficult" was borrowed for its sound.

乗.note: 乗 is a person, 大, climbing a tree, 木, feet showing: to mount, to ride.

西.note: 西 is read as a bird's nest, taken for "west", traditionally because birds roost at sunset.
西.history: The oldest 西 comes in two shapes. The open-topped one has been read as a bird's nest, a word kept in 栖, to roost; the closed one may be 囟, the soft spot on a baby's head, which one early script wrote for "west". The old explanation joins nest and west: birds go to roost as the sun goes down in the west.

要.note: 要 is a person with hands on the waist, first "waist", now 腰.

南.note: 南 pictured a lidded vessel, borrowed for its sound to mean "south".

間.note: 間 was 閒: the moon, 月, seen through a gap in the door; 日 took its place.

決.note: 氵 because 決 first meant a river breaking through its bank.

余.note: 余 pictured a thatched hut, borrowed for "I"; Japan also writes 餘, surplus, with it.

重.note: 重 is a person carrying a sack, 東, standing on the ground: heavy.

働.note: 働 was made in Japan from 動, move, with 亻 added; it was read はたらく by 1503.

医.note: 医 is arrows, 矢, put away in a case; Japan uses it for 醫, which held a wine jar, 酉.

発.note: 発 first pictured a bow shooting an arrow; a hand added later became the 癶 on top.

参.note: 参's three 厶 were three stars of a constellation shining over a person.

文.note: 文 is a person with a pattern tattooed on the chest, first "pattern", now 紋.

斉.note: 斉 pictured fruit growing in neat rows; it is not 文, though filed under it.

済.note: 氵 because 済 first meant to ford a river; finishing came later.

楽.note: 楽 is strings stretched over wood, 木: an instrument; 白 between them may be a thumb.

英.note: 艹 because 英 first meant a flower; excellent came later.

赤.note: 赤 is a person, now 土, over fire: the colour of flames.

色.note: 色 is a hand pressing down a kneeling person, first "to press", borrowed for "colour".

無.note: 灬 is not fire here: 無 first pictured a dancer, borrowed for "nothing".
無.history: 無 is a dancer holding ox tails in both hands, dancing to pray for rain; the tails and legs are what became the lower strokes and 灬. It was borrowed for "have none", and dancing moved to 舞, which adds two feet, 舛, below.

畳.note: 畳's 田 was once 日: three suns in one character were thought too much for an emperor.
畳.history: The old form had 晶, three suns, over 宜. The Shuowen says Wang Mang, who ruled the short Xin dynasty, thought three suns in one character too strong a sign and had them changed to three fields, 畾, giving 疊. Japan's 畳 keeps one 田 of the three.

僕.note: 僕 first pictured a slave carrying a basket, a tail drawn on to show low rank.
僕.history: The oldest 僕 is a captive at work: hands holding a basket for refuse, a punishment tool over the head, and a tail to mark someone counted with animals. The parts wore down into 菐, now a sound part, beside 亻. From "servant" it became a humble "I", and Japanese boys and men still say 僕 for "me".

共.note: 共 is two hands holding up an object; its 廿 is that object, not twenty.

亜.note: 亜 pictured a cross-shaped tomb seen from above; it spells the A of 亜細亜, Asia.

円.note: 円 is 圓 written fast: the 員 inside became one stroke, and the box's floor rose to meet it.
円.history: 円 began as 圓, a round border, 囗, around 員, itself an old word for round. From the start of the Meiji period people wrote the 員 as a single stroke, and over time the bottom of the box crept up until, by the post-war reform, it sat at or above the middle, leaving 円. That is the character of the yen.

典.note: 典 is 冊, a book, on a table whose legs are the 八 below; it is not 曲.

民.note: 民's oldest form is an eye pierced by a sharp point, linked to dim sight; 眠 keeps the eye.

舟.note: 舟 is a boat; inside other kanji it often turns into 月.

来.note: 来 first pictured wheat, an ear on its stalk, borrowed for "come" in the oldest script.
来.history: The old form 來 is a wheat plant: the ear at the top, leaves rising, stem and roots below. It was borrowed for "to come" in the oldest inscriptions, and the plant itself moved to 麦 (old 麥). Scribes once added a foot to keep "come" apart, but the plain picture won. An old dictionary ties the two together, saying wheat came from heaven, and wheat did reach China from far to the west.

気.note: 気's 㐅 replaced 米, rice: 氣 first meant food given to guests; vapour came from 气.

妻.note: 妻 is a hand, ⺕, grasping a woman's hair, read as marriage by capture.

声.note: 声 is the top of 聲: a hanging stone chime being struck, heard by an ear, 耳.

番.note: 番's 田 is not a field: it is read as an animal's paw print, or seeds in a hand.

為.note: 灬 is the elephant's legs, not fire: 為 first pictured a hand leading an elephant to work.
為.history: In the oracle bones 為 is a hand (又) on an elephant (象): putting an elephant to work, so "to do, to make". The hand turned into 爪, the claw on top of the old form 爲, and the elephant wore down to the strokes below and the 灬 of its legs. The Shuowen, written after the picture was forgotten, read it as a female monkey.

鳥.note: 灬 is the bird's feet and tail, not fire.

島.note: 島 is 鳥, a bird, on 山, a mountain, though the bird is there for the sound.

馬.note: 灬 is the horse's legs and tail, not fire.

驚.note: 驚 has 馬, a horse, because horses startle easily; 敬 gives the sound.

鹿.note: 鹿 is a deer: the antlers and snout became 广, the bent legs 比.

咲.note: 咲 was an old form of 笑, laugh; Japan uses it for flowers blooming.

鬼.note: 鬼 is a kneeling figure with a huge face, perhaps a mask; 厶 is a tail added later.

嘘.note: 嘘 means "lie" only in Japan; in Chinese it is to breathe out, 口 and 虚, empty.
